description: Columbus's 1492 landfall, what he discovered, and how he treated the Tainos of Hispaniola.
content_html:
Who Was Columbus and Why Did Spain Back Him?

Christopher Columbus was born in Genoa (in modern Italy) around 1451. An experienced sailor, he had spent years trying to find a royal sponsor for a westward Atlantic crossing. He was rejected by Portugal, whose experts correctly judged that his estimate of the distance to Asia was too short. Spain’s monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella agreed to fund his expedition in the 1492 Capitulations of Santa Fe, which promised Columbus the title of Admiral of the Ocean Sea, governorship of any new lands, and a share of any profits. Spain was willing to gamble because the investment was modest — three ships and about ninety men.

Key Fact

Columbus was promised the title “Admiral of the Ocean Sea,” governorship of any discovered lands, and a tenth of any profits in the 1492 Capitulations of Santa Fe. Spain backed him partly because the Treaty of Tordesillas blocked them from the Portuguese African route.

The 1492 Voyage

Columbus sailed from Palos, Spain, on 3 August 1492, with three ships: the Santa María (his flagship), the Pinta and the Niña. After stopping at the Canary Islands, he set out west across the Atlantic. The crew grew anxious as weeks passed with no land in sight — the voyage was taking much longer than Columbus had predicted. On 12 October 1492, a lookout aboard the Pinta sighted land. Columbus believed he had reached islands off the coast of Asia (which he called the “Indies”); he had, in fact, arrived in the Bahamas, at an island he named San Salvador.

Columbus explored further, reaching Cuba (which he initially thought might be the Chinese mainland) and an island he named Hispaniola. On Christmas Day 1492, the Santa María ran aground on Hispaniola’s coast. Columbus used its timbers to build a small fort, La Navidad (“the Nativity”), leaving thirty-nine men there — the first European settlement attempt in the Americas. He returned to Spain in March 1493 to a hero’s welcome.

Columbus returned to the Caribbean in September 1493 with a much larger fleet of seventeen ships and around 1,200 settlers — the first significant colonial expedition to the Americas. When he reached La Navidad he found it burnt and all his men dead, killed by the Tainos after disputes over food and women. Columbus established a new settlement, La Isabela, further along the coast and declared himself governor. He made four Atlantic crossings in total (1492, 1493, 1498, 1502), exploring the coasts of Central and South America and many Caribbean islands, but always insisting he had reached Asia.

His third voyage (1498) brought him to the mainland of South America near modern Venezuela. He wrote in his journal that he believed he had found a terrestrial paradise — a great continent, not a collection of islands off Asia. Yet he died in 1506 still believing he had reached the fringes of Asia. It was left to other explorers, particularly Amerigo Vespucci, to recognise that he had found a previously unknown continent.

The Tainos: First Contact

When Columbus landed on San Salvador in October 1492, he encountered the Tainos — the indigenous people of the Bahamas, Cuba and Hispaniola. Columbus’s journal describes them as generous, peaceful and physically impressive. On the day of first contact, he wrote admiringly of their hospitality. Within hours, however, he had noted that they “would easily be made Christians” and “would make fine servants.” His perception of them shifted almost immediately from curiosity to calculation.

Key Fact

Columbus kidnapped several Tainos on his first voyage to bring back to Spain as proof of his discoveries. During his governorship of Hispaniola (1493–1500), he imposed a gold tribute on the Tainos and authorised the use of enslaved labour, sparking violent resistance.

Columbus’s Governorship and the Encomienda System

As governor of Hispaniola, Columbus imposed a gold tribute: every Taino adult was required to deliver a set quota of gold or spun cotton to Spanish authorities every three months. Those who failed had a hand cut off. This system proved catastrophic. The island’s gold deposits were too shallow to meet the tribute; terror spread through the Taino population. Columbus also began shipping enslaved Tainos to Spain — Ferdinand and Isabella eventually ordered the practice stopped, as they were technically Spanish subjects. Columbus was arrested and returned to Spain in chains in 1500 after a royal inspector found evidence of misrule; he was stripped of his governorship but allowed to make a fourth voyage.

The foundations he laid were formalised after his departure as the encomienda system. Spanish settlers were granted an encomienda — the right to the labour of a designated group of indigenous people — in return for a commitment to protect and Christianise them. In practice it was forced labour with a religious veneer. The Taino population of Hispaniola, estimated at between 250,000 and 500,000 in 1492, had collapsed catastrophically within decades, killed by disease, overwork and violence.

For centuries, Columbus was celebrated as a heroic discoverer who brought the Americas into contact with the wider world. In the late twentieth century, particularly around the 500th anniversary in 1992, historians and indigenous activists challenged this narrative. The “discovery” framing erases the millions of people who already lived in the Americas. Columbus brought not just commerce and Christianity but also disease, slavery and the destruction of entire cultures. Modern historians tend to describe his voyages as the start of sustained contact between the eastern and western hemispheres — transformative but deeply unequal.
exam_tip_html: For 5-mark source utility questions, always address three things: the content of the source (what it says), the provenance (who wrote it, when, and why), and your own contextual knowledge. A source showing Columbus admiring the Tainos on first contact is useful because it shows initial European perceptions — but you need to explain why provenance matters (Columbus was writing for Ferdinand and Isabella, justifying his expedition). For the 12-mark evaluation, you must both agree and disagree with the interpretation before reaching a substantiated conclusion.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Columbus made four voyages to the Caribbean (1492, 1493, 1498, 1502), landing first on San Salvador on 12 October 1492. He always believed he had reached Asia; he never recognised that the Americas were a separate continent.
  • Ferdinand and Isabella sponsored him after the Treaty of Tordesillas blocked Portugal’s African route to Spain; in return, Columbus was promised the title of Admiral of the Ocean Sea, governorship and a share of profits.
  • Columbus’s treatment of the Tainos evolved from initial admiration to forced tribute and enslavement; his governorship (1493–1500) foreshadowed the encomienda system that would devastate indigenous populations across the Americas.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the 1492 Capitulations of Santa Fe.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying a feature (Columbus was promised the title Admiral of the Ocean Sea / governorship of discovered lands / a share of profits). Two marks for a developed explanation of its significance.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Columbus’s treatment of the Tainos during his governorship of Hispaniola.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• He imposed a gold tribute requiring every Taino adult to deliver a set quota of gold or cotton; those who failed had a hand cut off.
• He authorised enslaved Tainos to be shipped to Spain (later stopped by Ferdinand and Isabella).
• He established the encomienda system, granting Spanish settlers the right to Taino labour.
• His policies contributed to a catastrophic collapse in the Taino population.
[2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the decline of the Taino population of Hispaniola after 1492.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies and fully develops a cause with evidence — e.g. the gold tribute system created impossible quotas; terror, violence and overwork undermined Taino society; disease introduced by Europeans killed those with no prior immunity; links cause to specific evidence from Columbus’s governorship.
Secure: Identifies a cause with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Names a cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague statement without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Columbus’s first voyage (1492) for Spain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that Columbus’s return to Spain in March 1493 created a claim to a vast new territory, triggered a second much larger expedition (1493, seventeen ships, ~1,200 settlers), and began the process of Caribbean colonisation that would eventually deliver huge wealth to Spain — links to specific evidence and explains the chain of consequences.
Secure: Identifies consequence with supporting evidence.
Developing: States a consequence with basic explanation.
Emerging: Brief point without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Columbus’s voyages for the Taino people.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses significance at the time (immediate violence, tribute, enslavement, forced labour) AND over time (collapse of Taino population within decades; encomienda system applied across the Americas; loss of culture, religion and way of life). Develops argument with specific evidence.
Secure: Addresses significance with relevant evidence; may lack full over-time analysis.
Developing: Describes impacts without fully analysing significance.
Emerging: Brief or general points only.

practice_questions.text: 'Columbus’s primary motive for the 1492 voyage was personal glory rather than service to Spain.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the interpretation:
• Columbus negotiated aggressively for the title Admiral of the Ocean Sea, governorship and a share of profits — personal rewards, not national service.
• He continued to claim he had reached Asia even when evidence suggested otherwise — protecting his status.
• He resisted sharing credit and authority with others in the colony.

Arguments challenging the interpretation:
• Spain had a clear national interest in finding an alternative route to Asia after Portugal monopolised the African route.
• Ferdinand and Isabella framed the expedition in religious terms — spreading Christianity — and Columbus shared this stated motive.
• The economic rationale (spice trade, trade routes) was a national as well as personal driver.

Mastering: Sustained argument, agrees AND disagrees with evidence, reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some relevant points, limited judgement.
Emerging: Descriptive response without evaluating the interpretation.

knowledge_checks.q: Columbus sailed from Palos, Spain, on 3 August 1492 with three ships: the Santa María, the Pinta and the _____.
Columbus was arrested and stripped of his governorship of Hispaniola in _____ after a royal inspector found evidence of misrule.
Match each person or group to their role in Columbus's story:
right: Spanish monarchs who funded the 1492 expedition
Indigenous Caribbean people first encountered by Columbus
Explorer who recognised the Americas as a separate continent

flashcard_questions.q: When did Columbus first land in the Caribbean?
What was the name of Columbus's flagship on the 1492 voyage?
What island did Columbus name Hispaniola?
flashcard_questions.a: The Caribbean island that is today Haiti and the Dominican Republic.

flashcard_questions.q: What was Columbus promised in the 1492 Capitulations of Santa Fe?
flashcard_questions.a: The title Admiral of the Ocean Sea, governorship of new lands, and a share of profits.

flashcard_questions.q: How many Atlantic crossings did Columbus make in total?

flashcard_questions.a: A colonial labour system granting Spanish settlers the right to extract labour from indigenous people.
The indigenous Arawakan-speaking people of the Caribbean, first encountered by Columbus in 1492.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened to Columbus's first settlement, La Navidad, when he returned in 1493?
flashcard_questions.a: It had been burnt and all thirty-nine men killed by the Tainos after disputes.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was Columbus arrested and removed from Hispaniola in 1500?
flashcard_questions.a: A royal inspector found evidence of misrule, including violent treatment of colonists and indigenous people.

flashcard_questions.q: Columbus died in 1506 believing he had reached which part of the world?
What tribute did Columbus impose on the Tainos on Hispaniola?
flashcard_questions.a: Every adult had to deliver a set quota of gold or cotton; those who failed could have a hand cut off.

flashcard_questions.q: How many settlers did Columbus bring on his second voyage in 1493?

glossary_terms.definition: Genoese-born explorer (c.1451–1506) who led the 1492 Spanish expedition to the Caribbean, believing he had found a westward route to Asia.
The joint monarchs of Spain who completed the Reconquista and sponsored Columbus's first voyage in 1492.
The Caribbean island (modern Haiti and the Dominican Republic) where Columbus established the first permanent European settlement in the Americas.
The indigenous Arawakan-speaking people of the Caribbean islands, including Hispaniola, who were the first to make contact with Columbus in 1492.
A labour system in Spanish colonial America in which Spanish settlers were granted the right to extract labour and tribute from indigenous people.
